title: How are governments using AI? New evidence from around the world
gist: A World Bank survey of governments in 60 economies for the World Development Report 2026 finds AI adoption in government is broad but shallow — 44% of internal use is individual public servants doing ad hoc tasks — and that nearly two-thirds of governments provide generative AI access while only 39% have ministry-wide guidelines, creating 'shadow AI'; data quality is the top barrier at every income level.

insights.claim: Most governments surveyed report using AI in some form, but 44 percent of governments' internal AI use consists of individual public servants using AI for ad hoc tasks such as searching for information, summarizing documents or getting simple assistance.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Headline government AI adoption numbers overstate institutional capability; the addressable market for enterprise-grade gov AI is still largely unbuilt.
insights.locator: AI adoption is broad—but still shallow

insights.claim: When AI stays at the individual level, productivity benefits remain with individual users rather than the institution, whereas integrating AI into formal workflows lets governments establish common processes, monitor performance, manage risks and accumulate organizational knowledge.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Distinguishes seat-license revenue from workflow-integration revenue — the latter is where durable public-sector AI contracts will sit.
insights.locator: Giving individual employees access to generative AI

insights.claim: Ad hoc AI use is most pronounced in lower-income economies, but even among upper-middle- and high-income economies about one-third of governments report their internal AI use remains ad hoc.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Rich-country governments are barely ahead on depth of integration, narrowing the perceived gap in public-sector AI maturity.
insights.locator: This pattern is particularly pronounced in lower-income economies

insights.claim: The survey collected information directly from governments in 60 economies across all income levels, including central digital agencies, ministries and the officials responsible for management information systems.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: First-party government-reported cross-country baseline on public-sector AI, useful as a reference series for tracking adoption.
insights.locator: New evidence from the AI and Data for Better Governance Survey

themes.theme: Income is not destiny for government AI

insights.claim: Meaningful government AI innovation is not confined to high-income economies: the Philippines uses predictive AI to identify taxpayers at risk of under-declaring income and Thailand uses AI to detect tuberculosis and lung cancer from chest X-rays.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Emerging-market governments are deploying AI in revenue collection and diagnostics — high-value use cases and a real procurement channel.
insights.locator: Innovation is not confined to rich countries

insights.claim: Uganda has developed an AI assistant to answer human-resource queries inside its electronic document management system, the Democratic Republic of Congo uses an AI system to help correct state examinations, and Burkina Faso has built an assistant that helps citizens navigate the legal corpus plus AI applications for copyright monitoring.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Low-income governments are already past pilots in document, exam and legal-corpus applications, which resets assumptions about where gov-tech demand originates.
insights.locator: Uganda has developed an AI assistant

themes.theme: Barriers diverge sharply by income level

insights.claim: Data quality and availability are among the most commonly reported barriers to AI adoption across all country income levels, in rich and poor economies alike, because without accurate, accessible and interoperable government data even sophisticated AI tools have limited material to work with.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: The binding constraint on government AI is data infrastructure, so data plumbing vendors may capture spend before model vendors do.
insights.quote: AI cannot compensate automatically for weak government systems.
insights.locator: AI is only as good as the ecosystem around it

insights.claim: In low-income economies 58 percent of governments identify the lack of AI policies, guidelines, frameworks or standards as one of their three biggest barriers to adoption, while none of the high-income economies in the sample identify this as a major barrier.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A stark, quantified capability gap in AI governance frameworks that donor and technical-assistance money is likely to target.

insights.claim: Sixty-five percent of high-income economies identify privacy and ethical concerns as a major barrier to government AI adoption, compared with 19 percent of low-income economies, with legacy IT systems, interoperability and specialized talent shortages also more prominent in richer countries.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Rich-country public-sector AI deployment is gated by privacy law and legacy estates, which slows adoption relative to leapfrogging peers.
insights.locator: High-income economies have moved on to a different set of problems

insights.claim: There is no single AI-readiness checklist that applies equally everywhere; governments need different complements depending on where they are starting.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Invalidates one-size-fits-all AI-readiness indices and standardized advisory products sold to governments.
insights.quote: This suggests there is no single AI-readiness checklist that applies equally everywhere.
insights.locator: This suggests there is no single AI-readiness checklist

insights.claim: Nearly two-thirds of governments report providing public servants with licenses or official access to generative AI tools, yet only 39 percent have formal ministry-wide guidelines governing their use and another 38 percent are still developing them.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A quantified governance gap in public institutions — a live data-leakage and accountability risk, and a driver of coming compliance tooling demand.
insights.quote: Access to generative AI is expanding faster than the rules governing how it should be used.

insights.claim: The resulting 'shadow AI' — public servants using AI tools without adequate institutional oversight or guidance — should be addressed not by halting experimentation until regulation is finalized, but by building mechanisms that turn experimentation into organizational learning.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Signals the likely regulatory posture of development institutions: enable-and-govern rather than pause, which favors continued procurement.
insights.locator: This creates the possibility of what we call “shadow AI”

insights.claim: Governments need explicit mechanisms to determine what data can be entered into AI systems, when human review is necessary, how outputs should be validated, and who is accountable when AI informs a government decision.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A concrete four-part control checklist that will shape public-sector AI procurement requirements.
insights.locator: Governments need mechanisms to determine what data

themes.theme: From adopting AI to building better governments

insights.claim: Governments should not focus investments exclusively on AI, because building public servants' ability to work with data, conduct analysis, interpret evidence and draw sound inferences improves decisions today while creating the foundation for effective AI adoption tomorrow.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Argues against AI-first public spending; analytics capacity is the higher-return and lower-risk allocation.
insights.quote: Moreover, governments should not focus their investments exclusively on AI.
insights.locator: From adopting AI to building better governments

insights.claim: AI will strengthen public administration only if it helps governments make decisions and take actions that are more informed, appropriate and effective, so AI adoption should be part of a broader effort to strengthen capacity to use evidence.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Sets the outcome test by which government AI programs should be judged, rather than deployment or usage counts.
insights.locator: AI will strengthen public administration only if

insights.claim: Four complementary priorities are proposed: invest in people and analytical capabilities including AI literacy, strengthen data foundations and digital public infrastructure, build organizational capacity to turn experimentation into learning, and place equal emphasis on governance and adoption.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A checklist for assessing any national government AI strategy and spotting which line items are missing.
insights.locator: Our findings suggest four complementary priorities
